svg.text: Your business runs on APIs. Who is keeping them in order?

g.text: WITHOUT GOVERNANCE
WITH APIHUB
01 · KNOWING WHAT YOU HAVE
Nobody can say how many APIs exist, which version is live, or who depends on them.
Knowledge lives in people's heads, spreadsheets and wiki pages that stopped being true.
When a key engineer leaves, the map leaves with them.
One searchable catalog of every contract: REST, GraphQL, events, DB schemas, AI tools.
Agents in your Kubernetes clusters discover what is actually deployed.
The catalog stays current without anyone updating it by hand.

text.tspan: The organization owns its integration landscape — not individual employees. Audit questions are answered in minutes.

g.text: 02 · CHANGES THAT BREAK OTHER SYSTEMS
A developer renames a field. Nothing in the process catches it.
Weeks later a partner integration or the mobile app fails in production.
Customers find it first; the fix takes a weekend; the meeting is about blame.
Every new version is compared with the previous one automatically.
Each change is classified — breaking, risky, deprecating or safe — before release.
CI can block the merge; consumers see exactly what will affect them.

text.tspan: Fewer incidents from integration breaks, predictable releases, lower on-call and support cost.

g.text: 03 · DOCUMENTATION AS A TAX
Docs are written by hand, after the fact, in a different format per team.
They are out of date the day they are published.
Analysts spend weeks per release re-describing what the code already says.
Documentation is generated from the contract and versioned with it.
One format, one place, one link per version — with an interactive playground.
Guides, examples and diagrams live next to the spec.

text.tspan: Documentation becomes a by-product of publishing. Partner integrations start faster with fewer tickets.

g.text: 04 · DESIGN REVIEW BY MEETING
Standards exist on a wiki page nobody reads.
Reviews happen in meetings and email threads, depending on who is available.
Inconsistencies surface late, when fixing them means rework across teams.
Standards are encoded as rules and run automatically on every publish.
Every version gets a quality score visible to all teams.
Architects review exceptions — not every file.

text.tspan: Shorter approval cycles, consistent APIs across teams and vendors, far less late rework.

g.text: 05 · TEAMS WAITING ON EACH OTHER
"Is it safe to upgrade?" is answered in chat, if at all.
Consumers postpone upgrades; producers keep old versions alive forever.
Releases need integration freezes and manual regression rounds.
Consumers see, per version, what changed and what is deprecated.
Any two versions or revisions can be compared on demand.
Producers and consumers work in parallel against a machine-checked contract.

text.tspan: Faster time-to-market for cross-team features; a clean deprecation path instead of growing legacy.

g.text: 06 · AI THAT KNOWS YOUR SYSTEMS
Developers ask AI assistants about internal APIs and get confident, wrong answers.
The assistant has never seen the real contracts.
AI agents are hand-fed documentation that is already stale.
The catalog is exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
IDE assistants and agents query real, current contracts and their history.
Your own MCP tool surfaces are versioned as contracts too.

text.tspan: AI adoption grounded in facts. Contract knowledge becomes an asset for people and machines alike.
